source.title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne
source.translator: Charles Cotton (edited by William Carew Hazlitt)
source.attribution: Michel de Montaigne, Essays of Michel de Montaigne (trans. Charles Cotton), Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: When you dance, dance; when your mind wanders, gently bring it back
cards.body:
Montaigne's simplest rule for living was to be wholly in what he was doing. When he danced, he danced; when he slept, he slept. He admitted his thoughts still drifted off. Walking alone in a lovely orchard, part of his mind would wander to outside business, so he would call it back to the walk, the trees, the quiet and himself.

That is close to what we now call mindfulness. The aim is not a perfectly still mind but a habit of noticing when you have drifted and kindly returning. A meal, a walk or a conversation becomes richer when you are actually there for it.
cards.quote: When I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep. Nay, when I walk alone in a beautiful orchard, if my thoughts are some part of the time taken up with external occurrences, I some part of the time call them back again to my walk, to the orchard, to the sweetness of that solitude, and to myself.
cards.apply_it: On your next walk or meal, each time you notice your mind elsewhere, name one thing you can see, hear or taste, and carry on.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne do when his thoughts wandered during a walk in an orchard?
options: He gave up and thought about business
He went home to write them down
He called his thoughts back to the walk and the orchard
He tried to stop thinking altogether
quiz.explanation: He accepted that his mind would drift, and simply brought it back to the walk, the orchard and himself.

cards.title: A day spent simply living is not a wasted day
cards.body:
We often say, "I've done nothing today." Montaigne pushed back hard. Have you not lived? Living, he said, is not only the most basic of your jobs but the most important one. Knowing how to steer your own life, how to rest well and how to behave decently is a greater work than writing books or winning battles.

It is a useful correction for anyone who measures their worth only by output. A quiet day where you looked after yourself, kept your temper and enjoyed some small things still counts. Life is the main event, not the gap between achievements.
cards.quote: What? have you not lived? that is not only the fundamental, but the most illustrious, of your occupations.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, instead of listing what you got done, write down three moments today that you actually lived and enjoyed.

quiz.question: How did Montaigne answer someone who said 'I have done nothing today'?
options: He agreed it was a waste
He asked whether they had not lived, which is the greatest occupation
He told them to work harder tomorrow
quiz.explanation: For Montaigne, living itself is the most fundamental and most illustrious thing we do.

cards.title: The shorter life feels, the more deeply you can taste it
cards.body:
Late in life, Montaigne noticed that most people let good times slip by unnoticed, the way we sleep without knowing it. He refused. When he felt calm or content, he paused to taste it properly, involving his mind as well as his senses, and gave thanks for it. Bad hours he let pass; good ones he lingered over.

Since his time was short, he decided to make it deeper rather than longer. You can do the same at any age. Savouring is a skill: slowing down for a good moment, noticing it and naming it makes it last longer in memory.
cards.quote: In proportion as the possession of life is more short, I must make it so much deeper and fuller.
cards.apply_it: The next time something pleasant happens, stop for ten seconds and say to yourself exactly what is good about it.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne decide to do because his life felt short?
options: Rush to finish as much as possible
Travel as far as he could
Make it deeper and fuller by really tasting it
quiz.explanation: He resolved to extend life in weight rather than length, savouring the good moments instead of letting them slip by.

cards.title: Much of what hurts us is the opinion we hold about it
cards.body:
Montaigne opens one essay with an old Greek saying: people are tormented less by things than by the opinions they have about them. If an evil can only reach us through the judgement we make of it, he reasoned, then some of its power is in our hands. We can look at it differently, or even turn it to good.

He was honest that this does not abolish real pain. But it is a useful first question in a hard moment: how much of this is the event, and how much is the story I am telling myself about it? Changing the story often changes the weight.
cards.quote: For if evils have no admission into us but by the judgment we ourselves make of them, it should seem that it is, then, in our own power to despise them or to turn them to good.
cards.locator: Chapter XL. That the Relish for Good and Evil Depends in Great Measure Upon the. Opinion We Have of Them ¶1
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing worrying you. Write the bare facts in one line, then the story you are adding in another. Which line is heavier?

quiz.question: According to the saying Montaigne quotes, what torments people most?
options: The opinions they hold about things
quiz.explanation: He quotes the idea that we are tormented by our opinions of things, so changing the opinion can ease the torment.

cards.title: Keep a small room inside yourself that nothing outside can take
cards.body:
Montaigne loved his family, his home and his health, but he warned against hanging all his happiness on them. He advised keeping a "backshop": a private room behind the shop of daily life, wholly your own, where you can talk and laugh with yourself. If you ever lost what you have, being without it there would not be entirely new.

Today that backshop might be a journal, a daily walk, a craft or a few quiet minutes each morning. It is not about loving people less. It is about having an inner place to stand that does not depend on everything going right.
cards.quote: we must reserve a backshop, wholly our own and entirely free, wherein to settle our true liberty, our principal solitude and retreat.
cards.apply_it: Choose one small daily practice that is just for you, such as ten minutes of reading or journalling, and protect it this week.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne mean by keeping a 'backshop'?
options: A private inner space that is wholly your own
A second business for extra money
A place to hide from family
quiz.explanation: The backshop is an inner retreat where we keep our own company, so our happiness does not depend entirely on things we could lose.

cards.title: Make friends with the thought of death and it loses its sting
cards.body:
Most people deal with death by never mentioning it, Montaigne noticed, and then are flattened when it touches someone they love. He suggested the opposite. Take away its strangeness. Let it come to mind now and then, at a stumble or a near miss, so it becomes familiar rather than a monster in the dark.

He found the thought stung at first, but with gentle repetition it grew ordinary and stopped troubling him. Many people today find a similar ease by talking openly about death, making a will early, or simply remembering that time is limited. It tends to sharpen life rather than darken it.
cards.quote: Let us disarm him of his novelty and strangeness, let us converse and be familiar with him, and have nothing so frequent in our thoughts as death.
cards.locator: Chapter XIX. That to Study Philosopy Is to Learn to Die ¶35
cards.apply_it: Have one honest conversation this month about your wishes, or write down what you would want people to know. Notice how it feels afterwards.

quiz.question: What was Montaigne's way of reducing the fear of death?
options: Keeping busy so there is no time to worry
Becoming familiar with the thought of it
quiz.explanation: He believed that making the thought familiar strips death of its novelty and so of much of its power to frighten.

cards.title: A full life is measured by how you use time, not by how much you get
cards.body:
Montaigne argued that the value of living lies not in the length of our days but in what we do with them. Someone can live a long time and yet live very little. Whether your life is long enough depends more on your will than on the number of your years.

This takes some pressure off and puts some on. You cannot control how many years you get, but you can decide how you spend this week. The question shifts from "how long?" to "how well?", and that question is always available to you, today.
cards.quote: The utility of living consists not in the length of days, but in the use of time; a man may have lived long, and yet lived but a little.
cards.locator: Chapter XIX. That to Study Philosopy Is to Learn to Die ¶117
cards.apply_it: Look at how you spent yesterday. Name one hour you would spend differently, and plan that change for tomorrow.

quiz.question: According to Montaigne, where does the usefulness of living lie?
options: In the length of our days
In the use we make of our time
quiz.explanation: He said a person may live long and yet live little; what counts is the use of time.

cards.title: Missing someone everywhere is a sign of how much they were part of you
cards.body:
Montaigne's closest friend, Étienne de La Boétie, died young after four years of friendship. Years later Montaigne wrote that there was no action or thought of his in which he did not miss him. They had been "halves" of each other, and he felt he was living on with his friend's share.

If you are grieving, that feeling of absence in ordinary moments is not a failure to cope. It is the shape of the love you had. Montaigne kept talking about his friend, writing about him and honouring his work. Finding ways to carry someone with you can be part of grieving them.
cards.quote: There is no action or imagination of mine wherein I do not miss him; as I know that he would have missed me
cards.apply_it: If you are missing someone, write down one small, everyday moment when you felt their absence, and one thing about them you want to keep.

quiz.question: How did Montaigne describe missing La Boétie?
options: He missed him in every action and thought
He missed him only on anniversaries
He had forgotten him after a year
He refused to speak of him
quiz.explanation: He wrote that there was no action or imagination of his in which he did not miss his friend.

cards.title: Nothing comforts in loss like having held nothing back
cards.body:
Thinking about his friend's death, Montaigne said the sweetest consolation in losing someone is knowing you had no secrets or reserve with them, and that you shared yourself fully. He took comfort in that, and it made him open with his own family too: he wanted them never to be mistaken about how he felt.

This cuts both ways, gently. If you shared a lot with someone you have lost, let that be a comfort. And with the people still here, it is a quiet nudge to say the warm things now rather than save them.
cards.quote: there is no so sweet consolation in the loss of friends as the conscience of having had no reserve or secret for them, and to have had with them a perfect and entire communication.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Of the Affection of Fathers to Their Children ¶32
cards.apply_it: Send one message today telling someone you love what they mean to you. Keep it short and plain.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne find the sweetest consolation in the loss of a friend?
options: Having shared everything openly with them
quiz.explanation: He said the greatest comfort was the knowledge of having had no reserve or secret, and a full and open communication.

cards.title: Feeling numb after terrible news is a natural response, not coldness
cards.body:
Montaigne noticed that great grief often does not look like grief. Sudden terrible news can leave us stunned, silent and unable to move, because the soul is overwhelmed. Then, he observed, tears and words begin, and the soul seems to loosen and find room to breathe again. He quoted an old line: light griefs can speak, deep sorrows are dumb.

If you or someone you love went blank after a loss, that is a common human reaction. Feelings may come later and in waves. Be patient with the silence, and with the tears when they come.
cards.quote: the violence and impression of an excessive grief must of necessity astonish the soul, and wholly deprive her of her ordinary functions
cards.apply_it: If someone near you is grieving quietly, offer company without asking them to talk. Sitting together is enough.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne say excessive grief can do at first?
options: Stun the soul and stop its ordinary functions
quiz.explanation: He described how overwhelming grief can stupefy us, before tears and words gradually bring some relief.

cards.title: Time softens grief by slowly filling the mind with other things
cards.body:
Montaigne called time the sovereign physician of our passions. It does not work by making us forget, he thought, but by gradually bringing new matters and concerns into the mind, which loosen the first sharp hold of a loss, however strong it was.

This is a gentle way to see healing. You do not have to push the memory away or decide to be over it. Life keeps offering new days, small tasks and other people, and bit by bit they make room alongside the grief. It is fine if that happens slowly.
cards.quote: time, which she has given us for the sovereign physician of our passions, chiefly works by this, that supplying our imaginations with other and new affairs, it loosens and dissolves the first apprehension, how strong soever.
cards.apply_it: Choose one small, gentle thing to do this week that is new to you, such as a short walk somewhere different, and let it simply be there alongside your grief.

quiz.question: How did Montaigne think time heals our passions?
options: It does not heal them at all
By supplying new affairs that gradually loosen the first pain
quiz.explanation: He saw time as a physician that works by giving the mind new things, which slowly dissolve the first hold of sorrow.

cards.title: When a painful thought grips you, change the scene rather than fight it
cards.body:
Montaigne confessed that he was once deeply hurt by a just grievance and might have lost himself in it. Rather than battle the feeling head-on, he found something new to absorb him. His lesson: it is often easier to change a fixed, painful thought than to defeat it. Put something else in its place. Variety relieves.

After a breakup, staring straight at the pain can keep it raw. Gently turning towards new places, projects and people is not running away. It gives your mind other things to hold while the hurt loosens.
cards.quote: I find it a nearer way to change than to subdue it: I depute, if not one contrary, yet another at least, in its place. Variation ever relieves, dissolves, and dissipates.
cards.apply_it: Plan one new activity or outing for this week that has nothing to do with the relationship, and invite a friend.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne find easier than subduing a violent, painful thought?
options: Changing it by putting something else in its place
quiz.explanation: He found it a nearer way to change the thought than to subdue it, since variation relieves and dissolves it.

cards.title: Books can be a steady friend while your heart mends
cards.body:
Of all his companions, Montaigne said books were the most reliable. They comforted him in solitude, eased idle hours and took the edge off griefs, at least those that were not extreme. When a troublesome thought would not leave, he only had to go to his books and they would draw him in and push it out.

Note his honest limit: for the deepest pain, reading is not enough, and other help matters too. But for the long evenings after a breakup, a good book can be a quiet, faithful refuge that asks nothing of you.
cards.quote: it comforts me in old age and solitude; it eases me of a troublesome weight of idleness, and delivers me at all hours from company that I dislike: it blunts the point of griefs, if they are not extreme, and have not got an entire possession of my soul.
cards.apply_it: Pick a book you have always meant to read and set aside twenty minutes this evening for it, phone in another room.

quiz.question: Which griefs did Montaigne say books could blunt?
options: Griefs that are not extreme and have not taken over the soul
quiz.explanation: He was honest that books blunt griefs if they are not extreme; deeper pain may need more.

cards.title: The deepest friendships cannot be fully explained, only lived
cards.body:
Asked why he loved his friend La Boétie, Montaigne said he could only answer: because it was he, because it was I. They had heard of each other before they met, and at their first meeting felt instantly at home together. Their friendship was not built on usefulness, favours or any one quality. It was simply a meeting of two whole people.

You do not need to justify your closest bonds with a list of reasons. If you have a friend like this, treasure them. If you do not yet, stay open: such connections are rare, and they can begin at any age.
cards.quote: If a man should importune me to give a reason why I loved him, I find it could no otherwise be expressed, than by making answer: because it was he, because it was I.
cards.apply_it: Tell a close friend one thing you value about them that has nothing to do with what they do for you.

quiz.question: How did Montaigne explain why he loved his friend?
options: Because it was he, because it was I
quiz.explanation: He felt their bond could only be expressed as a meeting of two people: because it was he, because it was I.

cards.title: Friendship gives a steady warmth that passion rarely does
cards.body:
Montaigne compared friendship with fiery romantic passion. Passion, he wrote, burns sharper and more eagerly but comes and goes like a fever. Friendship is a general, even warmth: constant, gentle and smooth. And unlike desire, which can fade once satisfied, friendship grows the more it is enjoyed.

This is worth remembering in any relationship. Excitement is lovely, but the even warmth of real friendship is what lasts. Couples who are also good friends, and friends who keep showing up, are drawing on that steadier fire.
cards.quote: Whereas in friendship, ‘tis a general and universal fire, but temperate and equal, a constant established heat, all gentle and smooth, without poignancy or roughness.
cards.apply_it: Think of your closest relationship. What is one small, steady habit, such as a weekly call or walk, that would feed its friendship side?

quiz.question: How did Montaigne describe the warmth of friendship?
quiz.explanation: He contrasted passion's fever with friendship's 'constant established heat', even and gentle.

cards.title: Learn to enjoy a chat with anyone, not just people like you
cards.body:
Montaigne admitted he could be picky about company and cold in casual conversation. But he admired a different kind of person: a soul with many levels, at ease in any situation, who could talk with a neighbour about his building or his quarrels and chat happily with a carpenter or a gardener. He thought it wrong to put on airs with people in humbler jobs.

Being able to meet anyone where they are is a real strength. It widens your world, makes others feel valued and usually teaches you something you did not know.
cards.quote: that can discourse with a neighbour, of his building, his hunting, his quarrels; that can chat with a carpenter or a gardener with pleasure.
cards.apply_it: This week, start a genuine conversation with someone whose work or life is very different from yours, and ask about what they know best.

quiz.question: What kind of person did Montaigne admire in conversation?
options: One at ease with anyone, from neighbour to gardener
One who only speaks with scholars
One who always leads the conversation
quiz.explanation: He praised a soul that can stretch and slacken and enjoy talking with a carpenter or a gardener.

cards.title: Agree in advance: whoever loses their temper first gets left alone
cards.body:
Montaigne knew his anger flared quickly. So he made a deal with the people he might clash with: when you see me get heated first, leave me alone, whether I am right or wrong, and I will do the same for you. Storms, he noticed, come from two angers feeding each other; they are not born together.

A pre-agreed pause works well in families, couples and teams today. Settle it while everyone is calm: if one person is flooded, the other steps back, and you return to the issue later.
cards.quote: I bargain thus with those who may contend with me when you see me moved first, let me alone, right or wrong; I’ll do the same for you.
cards.apply_it: Agree with a partner, friend or colleague on a pause signal you can both use when a talk gets too heated.

quiz.question: What was Montaigne's bargain with people he might quarrel with?
options: When one is angry first, the other leaves them alone
They would only argue in writing
quiz.explanation: He saw that quarrels grow from angers feeding on each other, so he arranged for the calmer person to step back.

cards.title: Our word is the thread that holds us together
cards.body:
Montaigne hated lying more than almost any other fault. We are bound to one another, he said, only by our word. Truth also has one face, while falsehood has a hundred thousand forms, so once lies start nobody knows what to believe. He added that liars need an excellent memory, since they tell different stories to different people and are eventually caught.

Trust takes a long time to build and a moment to damage. Small lies to smooth things over still fray the thread. Being reliably truthful is one of the kindest things you can offer the people around you.
cards.quote: In plain truth, lying is an accursed vice. We are not men, nor have other tie upon one another, but by our word.
cards.apply_it: For one day, notice any small untruths you are tempted to tell, even polite ones, and find an honest way to say it instead.

quiz.question: Why did Montaigne think lying was so serious?
options: People are bound to one another only by their word
It is hard to do well
quiz.explanation: He believed our word is the only tie between us, so lying breaks the basis of human society.

cards.title: Raise children by reason and gentleness, not force
cards.body:
Montaigne condemned violence in bringing up children. He believed that what cannot be achieved by reason, care and skill will never be achieved by force, and he had never seen physical punishment do anything except make children more fearful or more stubborn. He himself had been raised almost without it and tried to raise his own daughter with gentle words alone.

Modern research on parenting broadly supports his instinct. Calm limits, explanation and consistency teach far more than fear does, and they protect the trust between parent and child.
cards.quote: I condemn all violence in the education of a tender soul that is designed for honour and liberty.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Of the Affection of Fathers to Their Children ¶10
cards.apply_it: Next time you need to correct a child, crouch to their level, explain the reason in one sentence and give them a clear next step.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne say harsh physical punishment did to boys?
options: Made them more cowardly or more stubborn
quiz.explanation: He said he had never seen whipping do anything but make boys more cowardly or more wilfully obstinate.

cards.title: Don't hide your love behind a stern face
cards.body:
A French marshal told Montaigne of his great regret after his son died young. He had always kept a stern, distant manner, thinking a father should. Now his son was gone, believing his father had neither loved nor esteemed him. "For whom did I reserve the discovery of that singular affection I had for him?" he asked.

Montaigne took the lesson to heart and made a point of being open with his family. Children of any age need to hear and see that they are loved and valued. Do not save it for later.
cards.quote: For whom did I reserve the discovery of that singular affection I had for him in my soul? Was it not he himself, who ought to have had all the pleasure of it, and all the obligation?
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Of the Affection of Fathers to Their Children ¶30
cards.apply_it: Tell your child, today, one specific thing you love or admire about them. Say it plainly, without a lesson attached.

quiz.question: What was the marshal's great regret about his son?
options: That he had not left him enough money
That his son never knew how much he loved and esteemed him
quiz.explanation: His stern manner meant his son died believing he was neither loved nor valued, which the father bitterly regretted.

cards.title: Aim to be loved by your children rather than feared
cards.body:
Montaigne thought it foolish for parents to keep grown children at a distance with a cold, severe face in order to stay in charge. It rarely works, he observed, and it makes parents look ridiculous to their own children. He said that although he could make himself feared, he would far rather make himself loved. Command and fear, he warned, stop working as you age; the affection of your family does not.

Warmth is not the same as having no limits. But a relationship built on closeness and respect will outlast one built on fear.
cards.quote: Though I could make myself feared, I had yet much rather make myself beloved
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Of the Affection of Fathers to Their Children ¶24
cards.apply_it: Plan one relaxed activity with your child or teenager this week where you follow their lead and give no instructions.

quiz.question: Which did Montaigne prefer to be, as a father?
quiz.explanation: He said that though he could make himself feared, he would much rather make himself loved.

cards.title: Never correct a child while your pulse is racing
cards.body:
Montaigne was troubled by parents who punished children in a rage. Correction given in anger, he said, is no longer correction but revenge. Would we accept a doctor who was furious with his patient? His advice: when you feel your pulse beating and emotion rising, put the matter off. Faults seen through anger look bigger than they are, like objects in a mist, and things look different once you are calm.

Waiting a few minutes is not letting a child off. It means the consequence, when it comes, is fair and actually teaches something.
cards.quote: When the pulse beats, and we feel emotion in ourselves, let us defer the business; things will indeed appear otherwise to us when we are calm and cool.
cards.apply_it: Agree a phrase you can use, such as "We'll talk about this in ten minutes", and practise stepping away until you are calm.

quiz.question: Why did Montaigne say we should delay correcting someone while angry?
options: Because faults seen through passion look bigger than they are
quiz.explanation: He compared anger to a mist that makes faults seem larger; once calm, we see things as they really are.

cards.title: Let a child's own love of a book carry them
cards.body:
As a boy, Montaigne fell in love with Ovid's stories and neglected his set lessons to read them. A wise tutor quietly turned a blind eye, and Montaigne went on to read Virgil, Terence and Plautus, drawn by the pleasure of the stories. Had the tutor forced him back to dull lessons, he believed he would have left school with nothing but a hatred of books.

His conclusion was that nothing beats winning a child's appetite. Children who are allowed to follow what delights them often end up reading far more widely than those who are drilled.
cards.quote: had he been so foolish as to have taken me off this diversion, I do really believe, I had brought away nothing from the college but a hatred of books
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶147
cards.apply_it: Ask your child what they most enjoy reading or watching, and find one book on that same topic to leave where they'll see it.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne think would have happened if his tutor had stopped him reading Ovid?
options: He would have become a lawyer
He would have left school hating books
He would have learned Greek faster
quiz.explanation: He believed being forced away from what he loved would have left him with nothing but a hatred of books.

cards.title: To comfort someone, start by honouring their sorrow, not arguing with it
cards.body:
Montaigne was once asked to console a grieving woman. He noticed that arguing with grief only makes people defend it harder. So he did not tell her it was not so bad. He first showed understanding of her sorrow, which earned her trust. Then, little by little, he let the conversation drift to nearer and further subjects, and she grew calmer while he was there.

He admitted this only eased her pain for a time and did not reach its root. Still, it is good advice: listen and acknowledge first. Advice and distraction only work once a person feels understood.
cards.quote: a man should, at the first approaches, favour their grief and express some approbation of their sorrow.
cards.apply_it: Next time someone shares a loss, say "That sounds so hard" and listen, before offering any advice or silver lining.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne do first when comforting the grieving woman?
options: Told her that grief was foolish
quiz.explanation: He noticed that opposing grief makes it more stubborn, so he began by acknowledging it.

cards.title: Anger likes to defend itself, even against the truth
cards.body:
Montaigne warned that anger flatters and feeds itself. When we are angry for a wrong reason and the other person gives a perfectly good explanation, we often get angrier, now at the truth itself. He told of a Roman commander who sentenced a soldier for a supposed murder. When the "victim" turned up alive, the commander's shame made him even more furious, and he punished more people.

The lesson is to watch for that flash of irritation when you are proved wrong. Saying "I was mistaken" quickly costs far less than doubling down.
cards.quote: How often, being moved under a false cause, if the person offending makes a good defence and presents us with a just excuse, are we angry against truth and innocence itself?
cards.apply_it: The next time you find out you were wrong in an argument, say so within a minute, out loud, before explaining anything.

quiz.question: What happened to the commander when he learned the soldier was innocent?
options: His shame made his anger worse
quiz.explanation: His fury, fed by shame and spite, grew stronger, which illustrates how anger defends itself against the truth.

cards.title: Catch strong feelings at the start, while you can still steer them
cards.body:
Montaigne noticed that every quarrel and passion is weak and easy to manage at its beginning. At first we guide things; once they are running, they guide us. It is much easier not to get into a storm than to get out of one. So he learned to stop the first rush of an emotion and step away from a subject that was starting to grip him, before it carried him off.

Today we would call this noticing early warning signs: a tight jaw, a faster heartbeat, a sharp tone. Acting on them early is far easier than calming down later.
cards.quote: We guide affairs in their beginnings, and have them in our own power; but afterwards, when they are once at work, ‘tis they that guide and govern us
cards.locator: Chapter X. Of Managing the Will ¶90
cards.apply_it: List three early signs that you are getting upset. Next time you notice one, pause and take three slow breaths before replying.

quiz.question: When did Montaigne say we have the most control over a situation or passion?
quiz.explanation: At the start we guide affairs; once they are under way, they guide us.

cards.title: Your own past mistakes teach you more than any book
cards.body:
Montaigne said he would rather understand himself than Cicero. Our own experience, if we pay attention, is enough to make us wise. Remember how far your last fit of anger carried you, he suggested, and you will see its ugliness more clearly than in any philosophy book. Recall the troubles you have faced and how small things changed your life, and you will be better prepared for the next change.

Reflection turns experience into wisdom. Without it, we simply repeat ourselves.
cards.quote: whoever will call to mind the excess of his past anger, and to what a degree that fever transported him, will see the deformity of this passion better than in Aristotle
cards.apply_it: Think of the last time you lost your temper. Write down what set it off and what you would like to do differently next time.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne say would show you the ugliness of anger better than Aristotle?
quiz.explanation: He believed honest reflection on our own past anger teaches us more than any author can.

cards.title: A jolt of fear is natural; what matters is whether you let it decide
cards.body:
Montaigne admitted he still jumped at a sudden gunshot, and so did braver men. Even the Stoics, he said, allowed that a wise person may tremble at thunder and go pale with fright. The difference is what happens next. The wise person's judgement stays sound and does not consent to the panic, while for others the fear sinks in and they start acting according to it.

You do not have to stop feeling the first surge of an emotion. You only have to avoid handing it the steering wheel.
cards.quote: provided his judgment remain sound and entire, and that the seat of his reason suffer no concussion nor alteration, and that he yield no consent to his fright and discomposure.
cards.apply_it: When you next feel a jolt of fear or anxiety, name it ("this is fear") and then ask: what would I do if I were calm?

quiz.question: According to the Stoics Montaigne describes, what makes the wise person different when frightened?
options: They feel no fear at all
Their judgement stays sound and does not consent to the fear
quiz.explanation: The first startle is natural; the wise person simply does not let it take over their judgement.

cards.title: A well-made mind beats a well-stuffed one
cards.body:
Montaigne wanted a tutor for a young pupil who had "rather a well-made than a well-filled head." Knowledge mattered, but judgement and character mattered more. He complained that schools poured facts into children as if into a funnel, then asked them only to repeat what they had heard.

The phrase still holds. Being able to weigh evidence, ask good questions and decide wisely is worth more than a head full of facts you cannot use. When you learn, aim to build your thinking, not just your store of information.
cards.quote: a tutor, who has rather a well-made than a well-filled head
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶11
cards.apply_it: After learning something new today, ask yourself one judgement question about it: is it true, why does it matter, and how would I use it?

quiz.question: What kind of head did Montaigne want a tutor to have?
quiz.explanation: He preferred a well-made head, valuing judgement and manners above mere learning.

cards.title: Don't accept an idea just because a famous name said it
cards.body:
Montaigne wanted pupils to examine and sift everything they read, taking nothing on authority alone. Aristotle should carry no more weight than Epicurus or the Stoics simply because of his name. Lay the different views side by side, he said; let the learner choose if they can, and if they cannot, let them stay in doubt.

Comfort with saying "I'm not sure yet" is a mark of a good thinker. In an age of confident headlines and viral experts, sifting claims for yourself is a vital habit.
cards.quote: Let him make him examine and thoroughly sift everything he reads, and lodge nothing in his fancy upon simple authority and upon trust.
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶20
cards.apply_it: Take one claim you saw today and check it against two other sources before you repeat it.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne want a pupil to do if he could not choose between opinions?
quiz.explanation: He wanted pupils to weigh views themselves and, when unsure, to stay honestly in doubt.

cards.title: Admitting you were wrong mid-argument is a rare strength
cards.body:
Montaigne wanted young people to learn to give way to the truth the moment they saw it, whether in an opponent's argument or in their own second thoughts. Stubbornness and contention are common, he said, and found most in small souls. Correcting yourself and dropping a bad argument in the heat of debate are rare, great qualities.

It can feel like losing, but it is the opposite. People trust those who can change their minds, and you learn far faster when winning matters less than getting it right.
cards.quote: to revise and correct himself, to forsake an unjust argument in the height and heat of dispute, are rare, great, and philosophical qualities.
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶46
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, look for one point where the other person is right and say so out loud.

quiz.question: Which qualities did Montaigne call rare and great?
options: Correcting yourself and dropping an unjust argument in the heat of dispute
quiz.explanation: He saw obstinacy as common and the ability to correct yourself mid-argument as rare and admirable.

cards.title: Everyone you meet knows something you do not
cards.body:
Montaigne told young people to keep their eyes and ears open in every corner of a room. The most honoured seats, he observed, often go to those with least to say, while fine things said at the lower end of the table are lost. Learn from everyone, he urged: a peasant, a bricklayer, a passer-by. Even others' foolishness can teach you, by showing what to avoid.

This turns every encounter into a lesson. Curiosity about other people's skills and experiences is one of the cheapest and richest educations there is.
cards.quote: Let him examine every man’s talent; a peasant, a bricklayer, a passenger: one may learn something from every one of these in their several capacities
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶47
cards.apply_it: Ask someone today, "What is something you know a lot about that most people don't?" and listen properly.

quiz.question: Who did Montaigne say we can learn from?
options: Everyone, from a peasant to a bricklayer
quiz.explanation: He believed something useful can be learned from anyone, in their own field.

cards.title: Judge a decision by what you knew then, not by how it turned out
cards.body:
Montaigne rarely regretted past decisions. When something went badly, he asked whether his choice had been sound given what he knew at the time. Advice and decisions, he said, belong to their moment, because things keep shifting. Some of his errors came not from poor judgement but from bad luck and hidden factors no one could have foreseen.

Decision experts today make the same point: a good decision can have a bad outcome, and vice versa. Reviewing the process instead of only the result helps you learn without drowning in hindsight.
cards.quote: I do not consider what it is now, but what it was then, when I deliberated on it: the force of all counsel consists in the time; occasions and things eternally shift and change.
cards.apply_it: Think of a decision you regret. Write down what you knew when you made it. Was the choice reasonable then?

quiz.question: How did Montaigne judge his past decisions?
options: By whether they turned out well
By what he knew when he made them
quiz.explanation: He considered what the situation was when he deliberated, since the force of all counsel lies in its time.

cards.title: We tend to call anything unfamiliar "barbaric"
cards.body:
Writing about people from a newly encountered land, Montaigne made a sharp point about his own society: everyone calls barbarous whatever is not the custom in their own country. We have no measure of truth and reason, he said, other than the opinions and habits of the place where we live, so our own ways always seem the perfect ones.

The insight still matters. When another culture's food, manners or beliefs strike you as strange, pause. Ask whether it is actually worse, or simply not what you grew up with.
cards.quote: every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country.
cards.apply_it: Next time a custom from another culture seems odd to you, look up why people there do it before forming an opinion.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne say people call 'barbarism'?
options: Anything not in use in their own country
quiz.explanation: He observed that we judge by our own customs, so whatever is unfamiliar gets labelled barbaric.

cards.title: Prove you've learned something by using it in new ways
cards.body:
Montaigne wanted teachers to judge a pupil's progress not by what they could recite but by their life. Make the learner put a lesson into a hundred different forms and apply it to many subjects, he said, to see whether they truly understand it and have made it their own. Spitting food back up as it was swallowed, he added, is a sign of indigestion.

This is how deep learning works. Explaining an idea in your own words, finding fresh examples and applying it to new problems shows understanding far better than rereading notes.
cards.quote: Let him make him put what he has learned into a hundred several forms, and accommodate it to so many several subjects, to see if he yet rightly comprehends it, and has made it his own
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶16
cards.apply_it: Take one idea you are studying and explain it three ways: in your own words, with a real-life example and as a quick sketch.

quiz.question: How did Montaigne want to test whether a pupil understood a lesson?
options: By asking him to recite it word for word
By a written exam on grammar
By counting the books he had read
By having him put it into many forms and apply it to many subjects
quiz.explanation: Applying knowledge in many forms showed whether the pupil had truly digested it and made it his own.

cards.title: Gather from many sources, then make your own honey
cards.body:
Montaigne compared good learners to bees. Bees gather from this flower and that, but the honey they make is wholly their own, no longer thyme or marjoram. In the same way, a student should take ideas from many authors and blend them into their own judgement. What matters is not where each piece came from but what you have made of it.

When you study or research, do not just collect quotes and highlights. Connect them, weigh them and write down what you now think.
cards.quote: Bees cull their several sweets from this flower and that blossom, here and there where they find them, but themselves afterwards make the honey, which is all and purely their own, and no more thyme and marjoram
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶26
cards.apply_it: After reading on a topic, write one paragraph that starts "Putting this together, I think..." without looking at your sources.

quiz.question: What point was Montaigne making with the image of bees?
options: That we should work hard all day
That we should combine borrowed ideas into our own judgement
That nature is the best teacher
quiz.explanation: Like bees making honey, learners should transform what they gather into something truly their own.

cards.title: Study history for its lessons, not just its dates
cards.body:
Montaigne loved history, especially Plutarch's Lives, but warned teachers against drilling dates. Do not so much imprint the date Carthage fell, he said, as the characters of Hannibal and Scipio; not so much where a general died, as why it was unworthy of him to die there. Teach pupils to judge history, not just narrate it.

Facts are easier to remember when they hang on meaning. Asking why people acted as they did, and what you would have done, makes history both stick and matter.
cards.quote: he do not so much imprint in his pupil’s memory the date of the ruin of Carthage, as the manners of Hannibal and Scipio
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶52
cards.apply_it: When you next study an event, write one question about why someone acted as they did, and one about what you would have done.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne want pupils to focus on in history?
options: The characters and judgement of the people involved
The names of all the battles
quiz.explanation: He cared more about understanding the manners of Hannibal and Scipio than memorising when Carthage fell.

cards.title: Don't turn yourself into a pack-horse for study
cards.body:
Montaigne was against chaining young people to their books for fourteen or fifteen hours a day. It crushes the spirit, he said, and he had seen people made dull and unfit for company by an immoderate thirst for knowledge. He wanted learning woven into ordinary life instead: at table, in the garden, in conversation, in games and exercise.

Modern study science agrees that marathon sessions are less effective than shorter, focused periods with breaks, sleep and movement. Working smarter beats simply working longer.
cards.quote: I would not have his spirit cowed and subdued, by applying him to the rack, and tormenting him, as some do, fourteen or fifteen hours a day, and so make a pack-horse of him.
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶86
cards.apply_it: Plan tomorrow's study in 25 to 50 minute blocks with real breaks, and include one walk or chat away from your desk.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne say about studying fourteen or fifteen hours a day?
options: It is the best way to excel
It is fine for older students
It crushes the spirit and makes a pack-horse of the learner
quiz.explanation: He opposed tormenting learners with endless hours, preferring learning woven through daily life.

cards.title: An idle mind runs wild; give it something to work on
cards.body:
When Montaigne retired to his estate, he expected his mind to settle into peaceful leisure. Instead, he said, it behaved like a horse that has thrown its rider, galloping off and inventing all sorts of strange fancies. He likened the mind to fertile land left untended, which only grows weeds. A soul with no fixed aim, he concluded, loses itself.

This is a familiar experience: unstructured time can breed worry and rumination. A project, a study or a simple daily purpose gives the mind a field to plough.
cards.quote: it is like a horse that has broke from his rider, who voluntarily runs into a much more violent career than any horseman would put him to
cards.apply_it: If you have free time coming up, choose one small project to anchor it, such as learning a recipe or writing a page a day.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne compare his idle mind to?
options: A horse that has broken from its rider
quiz.explanation: His unoccupied mind ran wild like a runaway horse, so he gave it a task: writing.

cards.title: Avoid the harm you can; bear well the harm you cannot
cards.body:
Montaigne clarified what constancy, or steadiness, really means. It does not mean refusing to protect yourself. All decent and honest ways of avoiding trouble are allowed and even praiseworthy. Constancy is about standing firm and bearing bravely the troubles that truly cannot be avoided.

This frees you from false toughness. Ducking a blow, asking for help or changing your plans is not weakness. Save your endurance for what genuinely cannot be changed, and meet that with courage.
cards.quote: the business of constancy chiefly is, bravely to stand to, and stoutly to suffer those inconveniences which are not possibly to be avoided.
cards.apply_it: Take one current difficulty and split it in two: what you can still change, and what you must accept. Act on the first list today.

quiz.question: According to Montaigne, what is the main business of constancy?
options: Bravely bearing troubles that cannot be avoided
quiz.explanation: He said avoiding harm by decent means is fine; constancy is chiefly about enduring what cannot be avoided.

cards.title: A good life, like good music, needs both sweet and harsh notes
cards.body:
Montaigne wrote that we must learn to bear what we cannot escape. Our life, he said, is made of contrary things, like music made of different tones: sweet and harsh, sharp and flat, lively and solemn. A musician who only liked some notes could not play anything. We have to use and blend them all, the goods and the evils that are part of being alive.

This does not make pain pleasant. But expecting both kinds of notes can make the hard ones less of a shock, and make you more grateful for the sweet ones.
cards.quote: We must learn to suffer what we cannot evade; our life, like the harmony of the world, is composed of contrary things--of diverse tones, sweet and harsh, sharp and flat, sprightly and solemn
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent hard week. Name one good thing that was also part of it, and one thing the hard part taught you.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne compare life to?
quiz.explanation: He compared life to the harmony of the world, made up of sweet and harsh tones that must be blended.

cards.title: Fearing pain in advance means suffering it twice
cards.body:
Montaigne lived with painful kidney stones. Rather than constantly checking for signs of the next attack, he refused to add what he called the disease of fear. He would feel the pain soon enough when it came, he reasoned, without making it longer by dreading it. His line on this is short and sharp: whoever fears they will suffer is already suffering what they fear.

Worrying about something that may never happen spends your peace now. Prepare sensibly where you can, then let the future arrive when it arrives.
cards.quote: He who fears he shall suffer, already suffers what he fears.
cards.apply_it: When a worry comes up, ask: is there one useful step I can take now? If yes, take it. If not, write the worry down and set it aside.

quiz.question: Why did Montaigne avoid anxiously monitoring his illness?
options: He did not care about his health
Fearing future suffering only adds suffering now
quiz.explanation: He believed that one who fears suffering already suffers what he fears, so dread only adds to the pain.

cards.title: Take on others' problems with your hands, not your heart and lungs
cards.body:
When Montaigne took charge of other people's affairs, he promised to take them in hand, but not into his lungs and liver: to work hard on them without letting them consume him. He saw people who poured themselves into every cause and lived only in bustle. They seemed, he said, as useful to their friends as they were troublesome to themselves.

This is healthy boundary-setting. You can care deeply and work well without making every problem your own inner storm. You will often help more, and last longer, for it.
cards.quote: I have promised to take them in hand, but not into my lungs and liver; to take them upon me, not to incorporate them
cards.locator: Chapter X. Of Managing the Will ¶4
cards.apply_it: Pick one problem you are carrying for someone else. Write down what is truly yours to do, and let the rest go back to them.

quiz.question: How did Montaigne approach other people's affairs?
options: He refused to help at all
He made them his main passion
He took them in hand but not into his heart, working without being consumed
quiz.explanation: He would take pains over them but not let them get inside him and disturb his peace.

cards.title: Keep planting your cabbages; you don't need to finish everything
cards.body:
Montaigne wanted to keep busy and engaged in life's ordinary tasks right to the end. Let death find me planting my cabbages, he wrote, unbothered by it, and even less bothered that my garden is not finished. He pitied a man who, dying, complained mostly that he would not complete the history he was writing.

There is freedom in this. Do the work in front of you with care, but do not tie your peace to finishing every project. A life is never fully tidied up, and it does not need to be to have been well lived.
cards.quote: let death take me planting my cabbages, indifferent to him, and still less of my gardens not being finished.
cards.locator: Chapter XIX. That to Study Philosopy Is to Learn to Die ¶61
cards.apply_it: Choose one project you are anxious to finish. Today, enjoy doing one small part of it without thinking about the end.

quiz.question: How did Montaigne hope death would find him?
options: Planting his cabbages, unworried about his unfinished garden
quiz.explanation: He wanted to be found doing ordinary tasks, indifferent to death and to whatever remained unfinished.

cards.title: You are not your job title
cards.body:
Montaigne served as Mayor of Bordeaux, but he kept a clear line between the role and the man. "The Mayor of Bordeaux and Montaigne have ever been two," he wrote. He mocked people who puffed themselves up with every new position and could not tell bows made to them from bows made to their office.

We must play our parts well, he said, but as roles we have borrowed. Separating who you are from what you do protects you when jobs change, end or go badly, and keeps you humble when they go well.
cards.quote: The Mayor of Bordeaux and Montaigne have ever been two by very manifest separation.
cards.locator: Chapter X. Of Managing the Will ¶54
cards.apply_it: Write three things that describe you that have nothing to do with your work. Spend time on one of them this week.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne mean by saying the Mayor of Bordeaux and Montaigne were two?
options: He kept his role separate from his self
He split the job with a partner
quiz.explanation: He played the role faithfully but never confused it with who he was.

cards.title: Character shows in how you live when no one is watching
cards.body:
Anyone can play an honest person on a public stage, Montaigne wrote. The real test is inside, in your own breast, where everything is hidden and you can do as you please. Next comes how you behave at home and in everyday actions, where you answer to no one. He admired a man who offered to pay double to have his house made so everyone could see into every room.

Integrity is less about grand public gestures than about being the same person in private as in public. Small, unseen choices add up to who you are.
cards.quote: Every one may juggle his part, and represent an honest man upon the stage: but within, and in his own bosom, where all may do as they list, where all is concealed, to be regular, there’s the point.
cards.apply_it: Choose one small thing you do differently when nobody is watching, and do it the way you would in public for a week.

quiz.question: Where did Montaigne say the real test of a well-ordered life lies?
options: In what others say about you
In private, where no one sees
quiz.explanation: He said anyone can appear honest on stage; being upright within, where all is hidden, is the true point.

cards.title: Notice when you undervalue what you have just because it's yours
cards.body:
Montaigne confessed a habit he could not shake: he undervalued what he owned and overvalued things simply because they were foreign, absent or someone else's. His neighbour's house or horse seemed better than his own, though it was no better. Possession, he noticed, breeds a kind of contempt.

This is the grass-is-greener trap, sharpened today by social media. Seeing it clearly is the first step. Looking at your own life with the fresh eyes of a visitor can reveal how much is already good.
cards.quote: I lessen the just value of things that I possess, and overvalue things, because they are foreign, absent, and none of mine
cards.apply_it: Walk around your home or neighbourhood as if you were a visitor. Note five things you'd admire if they belonged to someone else.

quiz.question: What habit did Montaigne admit to?
options: Undervaluing what he had and overvaluing others' things
Refusing to compare himself to anyone
quiz.explanation: He noticed that possession breeds contempt, making others' things seem better than his own.

cards.title: Train the whole person: mind and body together
cards.body:
Montaigne insisted that education should not split the person in two. It is not a soul or a body we are training, he wrote, but a human being, and we must not divide them. Running, wrestling, music, dancing and riding were part of a good education alongside books. He quoted Plato's image of mind and body as two horses harnessed to the same coach.

Modern health advice agrees that physical activity supports mood, focus and learning. Whatever your age, looking after your body is part of looking after your mind.
cards.quote: ‘Tis not a soul, ‘tis not a body that we are training up, but a man, and we ought not to divide him.
cards.locator: Chapter XXV. Of the Education of Children ¶90
cards.apply_it: Add ten minutes of movement you enjoy, such as a brisk walk or dancing to a song, to a day when you are mostly studying or working at a desk.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne say education should train?
options: The whole person, without dividing mind and body
quiz.explanation: He insisted that we train a whole person, harnessing mind and body together like two horses.

cards.title: Moderation is the seasoning of pleasure, not its enemy
cards.body:
Montaigne loved life's pleasures and saw no virtue in despising them. But he also saw how overdoing them ruins them. Intemperance, he wrote, is the plague of pleasure, while temperance is not its punishment but its seasoning. He thought a wise person should be as skilled at enjoying natural pleasures as at any other duty of life.

Think of a favourite food, a glass of wine or a night out. Enjoyed in proportion, they stay a delight. Taken to excess, they bring regret. Moderation is how you keep enjoying them.
cards.quote: Intemperance is the pest of pleasure; and temperance is not its scourge, but rather its seasoning.
cards.apply_it: Choose one pleasure you tend to overdo. Decide on a moderate amount in advance next time, and notice whether you enjoy it more.

quiz.question: How did Montaigne describe temperance in relation to pleasure?
quiz.explanation: He called intemperance the plague of pleasure and temperance its seasoning, not its enemy.

cards.title: When a good habit starts harming your health, ease off
cards.body:
Montaigne loved books more than almost anything. Yet he warned that if too much study begins to damage our health and our good humour, the two best things we have, we should give it up. No benefit from books, he said, could make up for that loss. He recommended going only as far as pleasure lasts, and stopping where trouble starts to mix with it.

The same goes for exercise, work or any good habit taken too far. Signs like poor sleep, constant tiredness or irritability are signals to rebalance, and to speak to a doctor if they persist.
cards.quote: Books are pleasant, but if, by being over-studious, we impair our health and spoil our goodhumour, the best pieces we have, let us give it over
cards.apply_it: Check in tonight: is any good habit costing you sleep or good mood? Set one limit for it this week.

quiz.question: What did Montaigne say we should do if study damages our health and good humour?
options: Give it over, since nothing is worth that loss
quiz.explanation: He held health and good humour to be our best possessions, more valuable than anything books can give.
